claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Non-equilibrium cooling with limited atomic diffusion produces local nanoscale compositional fluctuations in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Local nanoscale compositional fluctuations promote heterogeneous nucleation of secondary phases from the BCC state.
Cooling rate modulates diffusion kinetics in the alloy.
Moderate cooling rates permit partial local atomic ordering.
Extremely rapid cooling suppresses the development of local chemical inhomogeneities.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing can fully equilibrate the alloy composition.
Incipient ordering and compositional fluctuations occur at interfaces between emerging secondary phases and the original BCC matrix.
Insufficient diffusional homogenization during cooling allows localized regions to deviate in composition.
Diffusion during subsequent thermal exposure enables secondary-phase precipitation or nucleation.
The secondary phases may include FCC phases or ordered intermetallics.
Rapid cooling largely preserves the high-temperature BCC state by preventing significant local compositional ordering.
Slow cooling or subsequent thermal exposure produces a higher secondary-phase volume fraction than the uniform BCC baseline.
Secondary phases will be spatially localized at regions of compositional fluctuation.
Rapidly cooled samples will remain predominantly BCC.
The as-solidified high-temperature BCC baseline contains minimal detectable secondary phase.
Complete homogenization during prolonged high-temperature exposure eliminates the driving force for heterogeneous nucleation.

A lack of statistically significant phase-composition difference between rapidly and slowly cooled samples, with both remaining homogeneous and predominantly BCC, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
